learn.intro: The New Deal brought relief to millions of black Americans and shifted their votes to the Democrats — yet Roosevelt depended on southern Democrats, segregation stayed intact and anti-lynching bills failed. The war years opened new opportunities and new pressure for change.

sections.title: 1. The changing pattern of black settlement and voting

blocks.p: The Great Migration from about 1915 moved well over a million black southerners to northern cities such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, drawn by industrial jobs and escaping Jim Crow. By the 1930s a significant minority of black Americans lived outside the South, concentrated in crowded urban districts such as Harlem and Chicago's South Side, hemmed in by restrictive covenants and discrimination in housing.

Migration slowed in the Depression, then surged again in the 1940s as war industries in the North and on the West Coast needed workers. Competition for housing and jobs produced tension, including the Detroit race riot of June 1943, in which 34 people died.

Voting: in the North, black Americans could vote. Traditionally loyal to the Republicans as the party of Lincoln, most black voters switched to the Democrats in the 1930s; by 1936 a large majority of northern black voters backed Roosevelt. In northern cities this made the black vote a factor Democrats could not ignore.

evidence: 1936: large majority of northern black voters back Roosevelt.

sections.title: 2. Pressure groups: the NAACP and others

blocks.p: The NAACP (founded 1909) campaigned against lynching under Walter White and began a legal strategy against segregated education led by Charles Houston and Thurgood Marshall, winning Missouri ex rel. Gaines v Canada (1938) on unequal provision for graduate education. In Smith v Allwright (1944) the Supreme Court outlawed the white primary in Texas.

A. Philip Randolph, leader of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened a March on Washington in 1941. Roosevelt responded with Executive Order 8802 (June 1941), banning discrimination in defence industries and setting up the Fair Employment Practices Committee (FEPC). The Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) was founded in 1942, and black newspapers ran the 'Double V' campaign — victory abroad and victory over racism at home. NAACP membership grew rapidly during the war.

sections.title: 3. Southern Democrats and the failure of Congress

blocks.p: Roosevelt needed the votes of southern Democrats, who held many powerful committee chairs in Congress through seniority. He would not risk New Deal legislation by openly backing civil rights. Jim Crow laws and black disfranchisement in the South continued.
Anti-lynching bills — the Costigan–Wagner bill (1934–35) and the Gavagan bill, which passed the House in 1937 — were killed by southern filibusters in the Senate, and Roosevelt did not push for them.

Several New Deal programmes discriminated. The Agricultural Adjustment Act (1933) paid landowners to take land out of production; many evicted black sharecroppers and tenants, and payments often went to landlords. The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) ran segregated camps. National Recovery Administration (NRA) codes allowed lower wage rates in sectors and regions where black workers were concentrated.

In the war, about a million black Americans served in segregated armed forces, often in labour units; the Red Cross segregated blood supplies. Units such as the Tuskegee Airmen proved their ability, and the contradiction of fighting racism abroad while facing it at home fuelled protest.

evidence: 1937: Gavagan bill passes House, blocked in Senate.
AAA (1933) led to evictions of black tenants.
About 1 million black Americans in segregated armed forces.

sections.title: 4. The positive impact of the New Deal

blocks.p: Relief and work programmes reached black Americans in large numbers because they were among the poorest. The Works Progress Administration (WPA) employed many black workers and ran literacy classes; Harold Ickes's Public Works Administration set targets for employing black workers on some projects and funded housing. For many black families, federal relief was the first time the national government had helped them directly.

Eleanor Roosevelt championed black rights: she supported anti-lynching legislation, and in 1939, when the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let singer Marian Anderson perform in their hall, she resigned from the organisation and helped arrange Anderson's concert at the Lincoln Memorial before about 75,000 people.

An informal 'Black Cabinet' of advisers, including Mary McLeod Bethune (Director of Negro Affairs in the National Youth Administration) and Robert Weaver, influenced policy. The number of black federal employees grew substantially. In wartime, Executive Order 8802 and the FEPC set a precedent for federal action on discrimination, even if enforcement was weak.

evidence: 1939: Marian Anderson at the Lincoln Memorial.
Mary McLeod Bethune, NYA Division of Negro Affairs.

misconceptions.wrong: Roosevelt was a civil rights president.
misconceptions.right: He offered relief and some symbolic change but avoided civil rights legislation to keep southern Democrat support.

misconceptions.wrong: The New Deal helped all black Americans equally.
misconceptions.right: Relief helped many, but the AAA displaced sharecroppers and the NRA and CCC built in discrimination.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of the influence of southern Democrats.
evidence.model: Southern filibusters killed the Costigan–Wagner (1934–35) and Gavagan (1937) anti-lynching bills; seniority gave southern Democrats key committee chairs.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of positive federal action 1933–45.
evidence.model: WPA jobs and literacy classes; PWA employment targets; the Black Cabinet; Executive Order 8802 and the FEPC (1941).

flashcards.q: Why did black voters switch to the Democrats in the 1930s?
flashcards.a: New Deal relief and jobs reached poor black families; Eleanor Roosevelt's visible support.
Migration slowed in the Depression, then surged to northern and western war-industry cities in the 1940s; crowded segregated neighbourhoods.

flashcards.q: What was the NAACP's legal strategy?
flashcards.a: Challenge unequal provision in education through the courts (Houston, Marshall) — e.g. Gaines v Canada (1938).

flashcards.q: Give three ways New Deal agencies discriminated.
flashcards.a: AAA evictions; segregated CCC camps; NRA lower wage rates for black-dominated jobs.

flashcards.q: What was the position of black servicemen in WWII?
flashcards.a: About a million served in segregated units, often in labour roles; some combat units like the Tuskegee Airmen.
Informal black advisers to the administration, including Bethune and Weaver.
First major federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction — won by the threat of mass protest.

checklist.text: I can explain changes in black settlement and voting patterns, 1933–45.
I can assess the impact of pressure groups, including the NAACP.
I can judge the significance of southern Democrat influence and Congress's failure to address black grievances.
I can explain the effects of the AAA, CCC and NRA on black Americans.
I can evaluate the positive impact of the New Deal, Eleanor Roosevelt and wartime federal policy.
